claims.text: Q235 steel in the pre-exposure state has a naturally formed native oxide film.
The native oxide layer on pre-exposure Q235 steel consists primarily of Fe2O3 and Fe3O4.
At room temperature, the native oxide acts as a protective corrosion barrier.
At room temperature, the native oxide is stable, adherent, and of low porosity.
The stable room-temperature native oxide retards corrosive attack.
Exposure to aggressive salts at 700–900 °C causes phase transformations and/or morphological changes in the native oxide.
High-temperature oxide degradation may include increased porosity, cracking, or spallation.
Thermal stresses and salt-induced reactions alter the oxide's phase composition and morphology.
Possible high-temperature transformations include conversion of magnetite to more porous hematite or formation of non-protective spinel phases.
Phase and morphological degradation compromise oxide integrity and accelerate corrosion.
Room-temperature salt exposure will produce minimal mass change and leave the oxide largely intact and adherent.
Salt exposure at 700–900 °C will produce detectable oxide phase transformation, increased porosity or cracking, and accelerated mass change.
A thermally stabilized or coated sample is expected to retain greater protection than unmodified Q235 steel during high-temperature salt exposure.
The proposed degradation mechanism operates when thermal activation drives oxide transformation under high-temperature salt exposure.
The proposed high-temperature oxide-degradation mechanism should not operate at room temperature or when an added coating stabilizes the oxide.
The precise transformations, critical loss-of-protection temperature, and relative contributions of thermal-expansion mismatch and salt-induced chemical instability are uncertain.
